pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Walk me through what `go test -fuzz=FuzzParseLine -fuzztime=30s` actually does. Where do the inputs come from, what makes one worth keeping, and what happens to an input that fails?
expected_points: starts from the seed corpus: f.Add values plus testdata/fuzz/<Target>/ files, both committed
mutates inputs and keeps the ones that reach new code paths — coverage-guided, not random
the generated corpus lives in the build cache, is machine-local, and is cleared with go clean -fuzzcache
a failing input is minimized and written to testdata/fuzz/<Target>/; committing it makes it a regression test that plain go test runs forever after
plain go test runs only the seed corpus, so -fuzz belongs in a scheduled job, not the per-PR one

questions.prompt: A fuzz body can't say `want == got`. What did yours assert instead, and why would 'it didn't panic' have been a bad property?
expected_points: a property is a claim true for every input: here, an accepted line has a known level and re-encoding it with Format parses back to an equal Event
round trip pins encoder and decoder to each other
returning an error is always allowed — the property only constrains accepted input
no-panic alone would pass a parser that silently returns nonsense; the test is only as strong as its property

questions.prompt: When does a golden file beat an inline `want` string, and what makes the `-update` flag dangerous?
expected_points: golden wins for large, structural output that changes as a unit and is reviewed as a diff
inline wins for small outputs, or when only one field matters — otherwise every unrelated change fails the test
-update rewrites the expectation, so it can bless a bug into the specification
the golden diff must be read in code review; the flag belongs in a _test.go file so the production binary never grows it

questions.prompt: How did you separate the fast tests from the integration tests, what's the alternative, and what does each choice mean for CI?
expected_points: testing.Short() plus t.Skip, with go test -short as the local loop — everything still compiles
build tags (//go:build integration) exclude the file from compilation entirely, so tagged-out code can rot unnoticed
the pull-request job must run the full suite; the short subset is a developer convenience
a CI that only runs the fast subset has decorative integration tests

questions.prompt: In your integration tests, what does `t.Cleanup` do that `defer` in the helper could not, and what is `TestMain` for? How do you know your fixtures are isolated?
expected_points: t.Cleanup runs when the test ends, LIFO, even after t.Fatal — a defer inside newTestStore would fire when the helper returns, before the test body
TestMain wraps the whole package run for genuinely shared, expensive setup; teardown must precede os.Exit because os.Exit skips defers
t.TempDir() is the simpler default when a resource belongs to one test
isolation means a fresh database per test and passing under -count=2 -shuffle=on or when run alone

questions.prompt: You faked the clock but used a real SQLite database. Give me the rule that decides, and say what a fake store would have cost you.
expected_points: double what you don't care about; keep real what you are actually testing
the clock is a stub because real time is slow and its behavior was never in question — and the fake makes the backoff sequence assertable at all
the SQL is the code under test, so a fake store would only test the fake: typos, NULL handling and engine behavior would go uncaught
cheap real things (bytes.Buffer for output, httptest for HTTP) beat doubles

questions.prompt: Your coverage report says 88%. What exactly does that number measure, and what would you do with the report?
expected_points: statement coverage: which statements executed, not whether anything was asserted
compound conditions and unsupplied inputs hide behind a covered line
use it as a finder — read the red lines and ask whether each untested branch matters (uncovered error paths are the classic finding)
chasing a percentage produces tests that execute lines instead of checking behavior

questions.prompt: Why does `Run` take args and three streams and return an int, instead of reading os.Args and calling os.Exit?
expected_points: os.Exit inside the code under test would kill the test binary
injected args/streams let a test drive the whole CLI in-process: feed stdin, capture stdout and stderr, assert the exit code
flags must be parsed into a private FlagSet — flag.CommandLine cannot be re-parsed between tests
the exit code is part of the CLI contract, which is what testscript-style tests assert
